title: Infrastructure as Code (Terraform)
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) ##### The server nobody could rebuild A consultancy's client ran their entire automation stack on one cloud VM, provisioned two years earlier by an engineer who had since left. The firewall rules, the managed Postgres, the DNS records, the object storage bucket, the IAM roles — all clicked into existence through a web console, one afternoon, undocumented. Then the client asked for a staging environment identical to production. Nobody could produce one, because nobody knew exactly what production *was*. The reconstruction took two weeks of reverse-engineering, and the result still differed subtly — a missing firewall rule that only surfaced during a load test. This is **configuration drift** and **undocumented infrastructure**, and Terraform exists to eliminate both. Systematic study of infrastructure-as-code practice (Rahman et al., 2019) identifies the same benefits practitioners report: reproducibility, reviewability, and the ability to recreate an environment deterministically. ##### HCL: resources, variables, outputs Terraform's language is declarative. You describe the **desired end state**; Terraform computes the actions needed to reach it from wherever things currently stand. ```hcl terraform { required_version = ">= 1.7" required_providers { digitalocean = { source = "digitalocean/digitalocean", version = "~> 2.40" } } } variable "environment" { type = string description = "Deployment environment" validation { condition = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment) error_message = "environment must be dev, staging or prod." } } variable "db_password" { type = string sensitive = true # redacted from plan output and logs } variable "instance_size" { type = string default = "s-2vcpu-4gb" } locals { name = "n8n-${var.environment}" tags = ["automation", var.environment, "managed-by-terraform"] } resource "digitalocean_droplet" "n8n" { name = local.name region = "blr1" # Bengaluru — data residency size = var.instance_size image = "docker-20-04" ssh_keys = [data.digitalocean_ssh_key.deploy.id] tags = local.tags lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true # guard against accidental `destroy` } } resource "digitalocean_database_cluster" "postgres" { name = "${local.name}-db" engine = "pg" version = "16" size = var.environment == "prod" ? "db-s-2vcpu-4gb" : "db-s-1vcpu-1gb" region = "blr1" node_count = var.environment == "prod" ? 2 : 1 } resource "digitalocean_database_firewall" "postgres" { cluster_id = digitalocean_database_cluster.postgres.id rule { type = "droplet" value = digitalocean_droplet.n8n.id # implicit dependency } } resource "digitalocean_record" "n8n" { domain = var.domain type = "A" name = var.environment == "prod" ? "automation" : "automation-${var.environment}" value = digitalocean_droplet.n8n.ipv4_address ttl = 300 } output "n8n_url" { value = "https://${digitalocean_record.n8n.fqdn}" } output "database_uri" { value = digitalocean_database_cluster.postgres.private_uri sensitive = true } ``` Two mechanics worth naming. **Dependencies are implicit** — because the firewall rule references `digitalocean_droplet.n8n.id`, Terraform knows the droplet must exist first and builds a dependency graph automatically. Explicit `depends_on` is only needed for relationships the code does not express. And **`sensitive = true`** keeps values out of plan output and CI logs, though note it does *not* encrypt them in state. ##### Providers and the plan/apply lifecycle A **provider** is a plugin translating HCL into API calls — AWS, GCP, Azure, DigitalOcean, Cloudflare, and hundreds more, including Kubernetes, Helm, and even GitHub itself. ```bash terraform init # download providers, configure the backend terraform fmt -recursive terraform validate # syntax and internal consistency terraform plan -out=tfplan terraform apply tfplan # apply exactly the reviewed plan terraform destroy # tear down everything in this state ``` **`plan` is the feature that makes Terraform safe.** It compares three things — your configuration, the recorded state, and the real infrastructure — and shows precisely what will change: ```text # digitalocean_droplet.n8n will be updated in-place ~ resource "digitalocean_droplet" "n8n" { id = "412886203" ~ size = "s-2vcpu-4gb" -> "s-4vcpu-8gb" } # digitalocean_droplet.worker must be replaced -/+ resource "digitalocean_droplet" "worker" { ~ image = "docker-20-04" -> "docker-22-04" # forces replacement } Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy. ``` Read every plan before applying, and treat `forces replacement` as a stop sign — on a database or a stateful volume, that line means data loss. `terraform plan -out=tfplan` followed by `apply tfplan` guarantees you apply exactly what you reviewed, with no drift in between. ##### Remote state and locking **State** is Terraform's record of which real resources correspond to which configuration blocks. It is the single most operationally sensitive artefact in the system. Local state files break teams in three ways: only one person has it; concurrent runs corrupt each other; and state contains **secrets in plaintext** — database passwords, generated keys — so it must never touch Git. Remote state with locking fixes all three: ```hcl terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "acme-terraform-state" key = "automation/prod/terraform.tfstate" region = "ap-south-1" encrypt = true # server-side encryption dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks" # state locking } } ``` The **lock** is what prevents two engineers (or a human and a CI job) applying simultaneously and producing an inconsistent state file. DynamoDB provides it on AWS; Terraform Cloud, GCS and Azure Blob offer equivalents. Enable **versioning** on the bucket too — a corrupted state file is recoverable only if you kept the previous version. Use **one state file per environment**, so a mistake in staging cannot touch production. ##### Modules A **module** is a reusable, parameterized bundle of resources — the mechanism that turns three near-identical environment configurations into one definition with three inputs. ```text infrastructure/ ├── modules/ │ └── n8n-stack/ │ ├── main.tf # droplet, database, firewall, DNS │ ├── variables.tf # inputs │ ├── outputs.tf # exported values │ └── README.md └── environments/ ├── dev/{main.tf,terraform.tfvars,backend.tf} ├── staging/... └── prod/... ``` ```hcl # environments/prod/main.tf module "automation" { source = "../../modules/n8n-stack" environment = "prod" domain = "acme.in" instance_size = "s-4vcpu-8gb" db_node_count = 2 worker_count = 3 backup_enabled = true } output "url" { value = module.automation.n8n_url } ``` Staging is then the same module with smaller sizes and `worker_count = 1`. Environments differ by **parameters**, not by copied code — which is precisely what makes them genuinely comparable and eliminates the "staging is subtly different" failure from the opening story. Pin module sources to a version tag when sharing across repositories (`source = "git::https://...//modules/n8n-stack?ref=v1.2.0"`), so a module change does not silently alter every consumer. ##### Drift detection and import **Drift** is any divergence between your configuration and reality — usually because somebody clicked something in the console during an incident. ```bash terraform plan -detailed-exitcode # 0 = no changes, 1 = error, 2 = drift detected ``` Run it nightly in CI and alert on exit code 2. Then decide deliberately: either the manual change was correct and belongs in the code, or it was not and `apply` should revert it. Silently accumulating drift is how you end up with infrastructure nobody can reproduce. **Import** brings existing, hand-built resources under management — the path out of the situation the consultancy was in: ```hcl # Terraform 1.5+: declarative import, reviewable in a plan import { to = digitalocean_droplet.n8n id = "412886203" } ``` Run `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` and Terraform writes matching HCL for you. Import incrementally, resource by resource, verifying that each plan shows **no changes** before moving on — a plan proposing changes means your config does not yet match reality. ##### GitOps: infrastructure through pipelines The mature workflow removes console access entirely: **all changes go through pull requests**, plans are posted as PR comments for review, and CI applies on merge. ```yaml name: terraform on: pull_request: paths: ["infrastructure/**"] push: branches: [main] paths: ["infrastructure/**"] permissions: contents: read pull-requests: write id-token: write # OIDC — no static cloud keys jobs: plan: runs-on: ubuntu-latest defaults: run: { working-directory: infrastructure/environments/prod } steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3 - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 with: role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/terraform aws-region: ap-south-1 - run: terraform init - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive - run: terraform validate - id: plan run: terraform plan -no-color -out=tfplan 2>&1 | tee plan.txt - uses: actions/github-script@v7 # post the plan for review if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' with: script: | const fs = require('fs'); const plan = fs.readFileSync( 'infrastructure/environments/prod/plan.txt', 'utf8'); github.rest.issues.createComment({ issue_number: context.issue.number, owner: context.repo.owner, repo: context.repo.repo, body: `#### Terraform Plan\n\`\`\`hcl\n${plan.slice(0, 60000)}\n\`\`\`` }); apply: needs: plan if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: production # manual approval gate steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3 - run: terraform init working-directory: infrastructure/environments/prod - run: terraform apply -auto-approve working-directory: infrastructure/environments/prod ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Edit .tf in a branch] --> B[Open PR] B --> C[CI: fmt · validate · plan] C --> D[Plan posted as
PR comment] D --> E{Reviewer approves?} E -->|no| A E -->|yes| F[Merge to main] F --> G{{Environment gate
required reviewer}} G --> H[terraform apply] H --> I[(Remote state
S3 + DynamoDB lock)] J[Nightly drift check
plan -detailed-exitcode] -->|exit 2| K[Alert] ``` Terraform and Docker Compose divide cleanly: **Terraform provisions the infrastructure** (VM, managed database, DNS, firewall, storage), **Compose or Kubernetes runs the applications on it**. Do not use Terraform to manage container lifecycles, and do not use Compose to create cloud resources. ##### Common pitfalls - **Committing `terraform.tfstate`** — it contains plaintext secrets. - **Local state on a team**, causing conflicts and lost updates. - **No state locking**, so concurrent applies corrupt state. - **Applying without reading the plan**, especially past `forces replacement`. - **Hardcoded secrets in `.tf` files** — use variables from a secret manager or CI. - **One state file for all environments**, so a staging mistake risks production. - **Manual console changes**, creating drift nobody detects. - **Unpinned provider versions**, so `init` silently upgrades and changes behaviour. - **No `prevent_destroy`** on databases and volumes. - **Modules with too many inputs** — if a module needs 40 variables, it is not an abstraction. - **Deleting resources from config to remove them from state** — use `terraform state rm`, or Terraform will destroy them. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: write Terraform provisioning a **VM, managed PostgreSQL and a DNS record** for self-hosted n8n, then **refactor into a reusable module with remote state and locking**. Do it in that order deliberately — write it flat first, feel the duplication when you add a second environment, then extract the module. The refactor is much more instructive than starting abstract. The mini project is that stack deployed for real, with a second environment created from the same module using different parameters. Then run the test that proves the whole premise: `terraform destroy` the staging environment and `apply` it back. If it comes up identical and working, you have genuinely reproducible infrastructure. If it does not, you have found the undocumented manual step. For the assignment, **refactor the config into a reusable module and configure remote state with locking**. Document the module's inputs and outputs in a README, and demonstrate the lock working — start an apply, then attempt a second from another terminal and show the lock error. That error message is the thing standing between your team and a corrupted state file. ##### Key takeaways - Declare desired state in HCL; Terraform computes the diff, and implicit references between resources build the dependency graph for you. - `plan` before `apply`, always — and treat `forces replacement` on stateful resources as a stop sign. - Keep state remote, encrypted, versioned and locked, one file per environment, and never in Git — it contains plaintext secrets. - Modules turn per-environment copies into one definition with parameters, which is what makes staging genuinely comparable to production. - Detect drift nightly with `plan -detailed-exitcode`, import existing resources incrementally, and route every change through a reviewed pull request with an approval gate.
